papers.title: Interdependent mode of RNA recognition by the interacting KH-domain proteins KhpA and KhpB
papers.abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) are central regulators of gene expression. In bacteria, two KH domain-containing proteins, KhpA and KhpB, are increasingly recognized as globally-acting RBPs, including in pathogens that lack well-studied RBPs, such as Hfq and ProQ. While KhpA and KhpB interact with various RNAs in diverse bacteria, their crosstalk and molecular basis of RNA recognition remain poorly understood. Here, we explored the mutual dependence between KhpA and KhpB in the food-borne pathogen Campylobacter jejuni. We demonstrate KhpA and KhpB interact in vivo, and their individual global RNA recognition is largely dependent on the presence of the partner protein. Using RNA co-immunoprecipitation, we reveal that KhpA requires a conserved KH domain motif for RNA binding, whereas KhpB relies on an atypical R3H domain. Moreover, mutating the RNA-binding domain of one protein compromises the RNA interactome of the other. Overall, we demonstrate an interdependent RNA-binding mode of KhpA and KhpB and anticipate that such KH-proteins have co-evolved to elicit joint RNA regulation in bacteria.

papers.title: Mechanistic prediction of fecal microbiota transplant engraftment and Clostridioides difficile colonization resistance with μODE
papers.abstract: Shotgun metagenomics routinely resolves microbial community composition down to the strain level via metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), but translating these static catalogs into mechanistic, time-resolved understandings of ecosystem dynamics remains a critical computational bottleneck. Here, we present muODE, a fully automated framework that converts MAGs into dynamical simulations of community metabolism equipped with a composable, literature-grounded ecology layer, fundamentally designed to serve as a mechanistic hypothesis-testing engine. It employs dynamic flux balance analysis (dFBA) coupled to a shared extracellular pool and integrates a composable ecology layer capturing pH inhibition, time-varying antibiotic pharmacokinetics, bile-acid transformations, and spore dormancy. To evaluate the core engine, we cross-validated the dFBA machinery to machine precision against an independent reference implementation. We provide native export to the established COMETS engine for third-party verification. Benchmarking against two independent experimentally validated datasets confirmed that while monoculture growth is robustly captured, overflow secretion and directed community composition remain strictly bounded by the flux-routing limitations of max-biomass FBA. However, when applied to rate-modifying ecological feedback, muODE mechanistically and quantitatively reproduces bile-acid-mediated colonization resistance against Clostridioides difficile. With a single rate parameter calibrated so that baseline deoxycholate matched its measured physiological concentration, the framework reproduced the uncalibrated antibiotic-induced collapse of deoxycholate, with the calibrated inhibitor concentration coinciding with the independently set inhibitory threshold of the pathogen and driving a ~44x shift in the simulated pathogen-susceptibility ratio; bile-acid transformation is represented in the composable ecology layer rather than in the genome-scale stoichiometry. Finally, applying muODE end-to-end to a real longitudinal fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) yielding 139 de novo genome-scale metabolic models, the framework successfully recovered the clinical direction of treatment. By transparently diagnosing the structural competitive-exclusion bias that limits precise compositional prediction, muODE motivates the necessity of community-objective extensions while transitioning microbiome modeling from descriptive taxonomy toward testable, quantitatively-validated dynamic hypothesis testing, laying the essential mechanistic groundwork for the predictive engineering of safe, targeted ecological therapeutics. muODE is freely available at https://github.com/cumbof/muODE.

papers.title: Mice immunized with N1 neuraminidase in a single cycle infectious virus or in a recombinant nanoparticle vaccine are protected against lethal challenge with highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 influenza
papers.abstract: The recent spillover of highly pathogenic (HP) H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b into dairy cattle and other mammalian species has been concerning. Vaccine candidates that can be rapidly synthesized and implemented are key countermeasures for protecting the human population against emerging pathogens. Here we examine the use of a pH1N1 virus lacking the genetic material for hemagglutinin (HA), limiting the infection to a single cycle (sciIAV) or Cobalt lipid-porphyrin nanoparticles decorated with neuraminidase (NA) of HPAI H5N1 (N1-CoPoP) as vaccine candidates. C57BL/6 mice that were inoculated intranasally with a single dose of pH1N1 sciIAV did not differ in serum NA antibody compared to uninoculated mice. However, mice that were inoculated intramuscularly with the N1-CoPoP alone or in combination with pH1N1 sciIAV had increased N1 IgG antibodies. Upon lethal challenge with HPAIV H5N1, all mice inoculated with either pH1N1 sciIAV or N1-CoPoP were protected from weight loss, unlike unvaccinated mice with substantial body weight losses that succumb to viral infection between 7 and 10 days post infection (dpi). Both pH1N1 sciIAV and N1-CoPoP immunization minimized viral infection such that only one mouse receiving pH1N1 sciIAV had detectable viral titer in the lungs at 4 dpi. By 6 dpi, no mouse inoculated with pH1N1 sciIAV and/or N1-CoPoP had detectable virus in nasal turbinates, lungs or the brain, unlike the high viral titers found in uninoculated mice. Both pH1N1 sciIAV and N1-CoPoP were protective and should be investigated further as alternative vaccine candidates.

papers.title: From dynamic transcripts to stable proteins: multi-omics revealed regulatory buffering of Candidatus Accumulibacter under cyclic conditions
papers.abstract: Enhanced biological phosphorus removal (EBPR) relies on polyphosphate-accumulating organisms that experience dynamic fluctuations in redox conditions and substrate availability. How these organisms regulate metabolism across molecular layers under cyclic operation remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated molecular regulation in a long-term, stable aerobic granular sludge system dominated by Candidatus Accumulibacter. We combined metagenomics, time-resolved metatranscriptomics, and matched metaproteomics across three consecutive operational cycles. Genome-resolved metagenomics revealed an Accumulibacter-dominated community encoding canonical EBPR functions. Time-resolved metatranscriptomics revealed extensive and reproducible transcriptional dynamics affecting hundreds of genes. These dynamics did not align with discrete EBPR phases or instantaneous environmental transitions, but instead unfolded gradually over the cycle. Despite pronounced transcript-level heterogeneity, aggregation at the functional level revealed strong consolidation, with only a limited number of KEGG orthologs exhibiting coherent temporal regulation. Quantitative metaproteomics revealed a stable proteome across EBPR cycles, with no individual proteins or functional categories showing significant differential abundance despite direct transcript-protein mapping and time-matched sampling. This indicated that transcriptional dynamics did not translate into measurable changes in protein pool size on the time scale of individual cycles, consistent with slow, growth-coupled proteome turnover relative to cycle duration. Together, these results support a hierarchical model of regulation in Candidatus Accumulibacter, in which dynamic transcriptional responses are buffered at both the functional and protein levels. This organization provides a plausible basis for stable EBPR performance under predictable cyclic operation and demonstrates how time-resolved multi-omics can be used to resolve regulatory dynamics across molecular layers in engineered microbial ecosystems.

papers.title: Isoindole-benzohydrazide derivative potentiates colistin activity to overcome resistance conferred by MCR-1 variants in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Polymyxin antibiotic resistance mediated by the mobilized colistin resistance (MCR) enzyme threatens the last-resort treatment of deadly multidrug-resistant pathogens, including Acinetobacter baumannii, and calls for urgent mitigation efforts. We used a multifaceted approach involving computational and wet-lab techniques to identify an isoindole-benzohydrazide derivative, JNAL-042, which potentiates colistin activity in an Escherichia coli MCR-resistance phenotype screening model. JNAL-042 lacked intrinsic antibiotic activity but potentiated that of polymyxin antibiotics at 12-24 mug/ml, as demonstrated by bacterial growth susceptibility screens. Cell viability counts and time-kill assays corroborated these findings, demonstrating complete abolition of MCR-mediated resistance by the antibiotic-adjuvant combination at concentrations mirroring those of empty vector controls. Post-induction treatment with this combination similarly prevented the propagation of the resistance phenotype, albeit at a higher antibiotic dose. This landmark study presents JNAL-042 as a promising antibiotic adjuvant to combat MCR-mediated resistance and offers a viable solution to preserve last-resort polymyxin antibiotics.

papers.title: Circadian phase alignment promotes survival under predictive oxidative stress
papers.abstract: Circadian clocks are endogenous time-keeping mechanisms that continue to oscillate with a period that approximates 24 h in the absence of cyclic environmental cues. This free-running period (FRP) varies from species to species and can vary within species across latitudinal clines. Because natural environments provide daily cues that reset circadian clocks to exactly 24 h, the importance of the FRP length is unclear. Using the cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus we show that the FRP length alters the alignment of a biological process with an environmental reference, known as phase angle of entrainment, across seasonal photoperiods, thereby repositioning stress response programs relative to the external environment. This phase relationship affects the overall fitness of the organism: strains that position stress-response programs to peak at the time at which the stressor peaks outcompete their early- or late-peaking counterparts. Our results suggest that the FRP length is selected for its ability to adjust the phase angle of entrainment across seasonal photoperiods: the wild-type FRP length was uniquely plastic in its ability to adjust stress-response programs to coincide with the stressor in all photoperiod conditions.

papers.title: Distribution and dynamics of Vibrio spp. and pathogen sequences among microhabitats and monsoon seasons in Singapore's coastal waters
papers.abstract: Marine infections are rising in temperate regions due in part to a warming climate. However, comparatively little is known about drivers of marine pathogen dynamics in the tropics where temperatures are high year-round. Vibrio bacteria are ubiquitous in both temperate and tropical marine environments, and many are important pathogens of marine organisms and humans. Here, we sampled an equatorial monsoonal site, the Singapore Strait, over 18 months and applied amplicon sequencing (16s rRNA V6-8 region) to three particle size fractions, qPCR quantitation of Vibrio spp., and generalized linear modelling with environmental variables to understand the factors that structure the Vibrio assemblage. We found that Vibrios represented the highest proportion of pathogen-related DNA sequences, with an assemblage composition influenced by microhabitats (size fractions) and monsoon seasons. Vibrio sequences were dominated by ASVs with highest identity to V. xuii, V. rotiferianus and V. caribbeanicus, and including ASVs matching agents of human disease in Singapore - V. parahaemolyticus, V. alginolyticus, and V. furnissii. Vibrio qPCR abundance was lowest in the largest size fraction (10-150 m), following planktonic DNA trends, even though pathogen-related sequences, including Vibrio, were enriched in this fraction. Temperature was a significant predictor of overall Vibrio abundance, but its effect was no longer significant after adjustment for monsoons, suggesting that the temperature association may reflect broader seasonal dynamics. Instead, effects of chlorophyll, ammonia, nitrate and suspended solids were more consistent within seasons. Furthermore, free-living and particle-associated Vibrios responded differently to environmental changes, suggesting that partitioning into microspatial habitats may lead to differences in their environmental sensitivity.

papers.title: Ethnic differences in gut microbiota composition and functional capacity persist over six years in the HELIUS multi-ethnic longitudinal cohort
papers.abstract: Background: Ethnic minority groups in Western Europe carry a disproportionate cardiometabolic disease burden not fully explained by conventional risk factors, and their gut microbiomes differ markedly from those of European-origin populations. Whether these differences persist over time has not been examined prospectively. Results: We followed 1,903 participants from six ethnic groups in the HELIUS cohort over 6 years, using faecal 16S rRNA sequencing across all groups and shotgun metagenomics in a matched Dutch and South-Asian Surinamese subset (N = 238 per group). The extent of microbiota compositional change over time differed between ethnic groups: Moroccan participants showed the largest change, while the Dutch and South-Asian Surinamese participants were most stable. Diabetes mellitus and medication use at baseline were associated with greater compositional drift. However, ethnic differences in composition were largely preserved across all six groups (16S: ethnicity R2 0.044 to 0.037; all 15 pairwise contrasts significant at follow-up) and in the shotgun subset (R2 0.047 to 0.037). At the species level, 61 of 78 ethnicity-associated species remained differentially abundant at follow-up. Alistipes putredinis, the species converging most strongly, was absent at baseline in 43% of South-Asian Surinamese participants, and the convergence was consistent with acquisition of this species by this group. At strain level, within-person strain sharing declined with follow-up duration but was similar between ethnic groups. Within hosts, 90% of A. putredinis populations were retained as the same or a closely related lineage, and within the retained subset, microdiversity increased in both groups. Ethnic differences in functional profiles persisted to a similar extent as those in composition, with limited convergence in fibre-degrading enzyme families (GH5_37, GH26). The total antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) burden in the gut microbiome declined similarly in both groups over time. Dutch participants showed higher baseline ARG diversity that converged toward South-Asian Surinamese levels, while class-level differences were predominantly stable. Conclusions: Six years of follow-up in a shared urban environment narrowed ethnic differences in the gut microbiome only modestly; assuming exponential decline, the observed change corresponds to a half-life of roughly two decades.

papers.title: Pulling water from a stone: subaerial biofilm water dynamics on porous solid materials
papers.abstract: Subaerial biofilms (SABs) are microbial communities that colonize air exposed surfaces in both natural and engineered environments, forming an interface between the atmosphere and the substrate. Often water availability is crucial for their metabolic activity and survival. While precipitation may contribute to SAB hydration, the dynamic processes of evaporation and condensation - closely linked to fluctuating temperature and humidity conditions - can be key determinants of water availability and they constitute the main focus of this study. We present a model connecting the water-related dynamics in an SAB, its surrounding ambient air and underlying stone/masonry. A central feature of the model is the increased water affinity of the SAB in comparison to the stone pore network. Based on thermodynamic principles, the model captures changes in liquid water content and availability by accounting for the evaporation and condensation at liquid-gas interfaces through gradients in water chemical potential. It accounts for the SAB's capacity to delay water loss by drawing water from substrate material pores to compensate for atmospheric evaporation. The proposed model is compared to prior experimental observations of water transport in limestone samples with and without SAB. Additional numerical simulations under variable environmental conditions demonstrate how permeability of the substrate layer may influence SAB water activity, and how the presence or absence of an SAB might affect water content within stone/masonry.

papers.title: Unsupervised decomposition of massively parallel TraDIS-Xpress fitness data from Escherichia coli identifies distinct functional and expression modules of antimicrobial resistance determinants
papers.abstract: Linking genotype to phenotype is a central goal in biology, one way to do this is using transposon insertion sequencing (TIS) where the fitness impacts of mutations across a genome are assessed in different conditions. Traditional analyses use comparison of each gene response independently in control versus test conditions, so a compendium of hundreds of test conditions returns hundreds of separate ranked gene lists. To unlock the potential information hidden within large data sets, we applied independent component (ICA) analysis to 754 Escherichia coli BW25113 TraDIS-Xpress samples. These samples included a series of antibiotic and other stress condition exposures. ICA is designed to identify hidden structure within complex data and to extract meaningfully linked components. In this analysis each annotated gene was resolved into a gene body and 198 bp 5' and 3' features so that expression effects driven by the transposon's outwards facing promoter enter the matrix separately from gene disruption effects. The decomposition returned 99 components, which we term fxModules, which were defined as containing elements with similar responses across the whole compendium rather than per any individual experiment. Of the 754 stress samples, the antibiotic arm included 110 samples derived from exposure to 14 separate agents at multiple concentrations. Many of these have been highly studied allowing us to explore the accuracy of predicted responsive fxModules. This analysis showed excellent predictive power of the approach and the fxModules responsive to individual drugs typically reproduced known mechanisms at a resolution superior to analysis of single gene sets. For example, exposure to fosfomycin identified responsive fxModules containing genes which are known to be involved in uptake of the drug, cAMP-CRP control and exposure to gentamicin identified oxidative phosphorylation split across three fxModules responding with different magnitudes and directions at different concentrations. This recapitulates recent work studying the landscape of E. coli genes sensitive to this drug with high precision without any prior knowledge of functional annotation. Similarly precise predictions were made for other drugs. Responsive modules also identified novel groups of genes and linkages beyond the boundaries of defined pathways as being responsive to various stresses demonstrating the ability to predict new genotype-phenotype links. Inclusion of the regulatory regions also resolved fxModules which were entirely contributed by promoter regions, for example for chloramphenicol genes responsible for efflux were identified by signals in intergenic control regions, and unidirectional insertions in gene bodies, a signal that a gene level matrix would not be able to predict with accuracy. These data show that ICA decomposition provides an efficient and accurate annotation independent approach to identifying sets of genes with related functional impacts in any given condition in the compendium. The functional modular association of genes also help in predicting gene functions of unknown genes based on the group function. This approach allows rapid identification of novel genotype-phenotype links and unlocks the power of multiple comparisons of transposon mutagenesis data.

papers.title: Genome-wide CRISPRi mapping of mycobacteriophage interaction determinants in Mycobacterium smegmatis mc2155
papers.abstract: Bacteriophages are highly specific predators of bacterial hosts, but the molecular mechanisms governing their entry across the structurally complex mycobacterial cell envelope remain poorly defined. Utilizing a genome-wide CRISPR interference library in the model organism Mycobacterium smegmatis against a phylogenetically representative collection of 70 mycobacteriophages, we mapped the functional architecture of host susceptibility determinants. This parallelized genetic screen revealed a spatial continuum of infection requirements spanning from outer leaflet surface structures down to deep cytoplasmic machinery. The four major outer membrane Mycobacterium smegmatis porins (Msp) emerged as the dominant candidate receptor family for 46 diverse phages, representing the first protein receptors identified within this group. Interrogating the asymmetric outer bilayer also implicated cell envelope glycolipids as candidate receptors for 14 phages, resolving into glycopeptidolipid sub-lineages. Beneath the mycomembrane, arabinogalactan functions as a candidate secondary receptor for 5 phages, while the inner membrane lipid transporter MmpL11 and the global nucleoid-associated protein Lsr2 represent determinant factors for 14 and 31 phages respectively. While physical deletions of major porins trigger spontaneous regulatory pathways that upregulate silent backup paralogues, acute transcriptional knockdowns circumvent suppressor accumulation, revealing unmasked single-gene dependencies. Structural analysis demonstrated that host determinant usage decouples entirely from whole-genome viral phylogeny, indicating that standard phylogenetic groupings fail to predict surface recognition profiles. Ultimately, mapping this host interactome reveals an evolutionary strategy where phages target highly redundant or abundant host machinery to exploit fixed physiological liabilities, presenting a robust molecular blueprint for the rational engineering of escape-resistant therapeutic phage cocktails.

papers.title: Metabolic reorganization shapes the dynamics of a water kefir microbial community
papers.abstract: Microbial fermentations emerge from the collective activity of interacting species whose relative abundances, metabolic functions, and environmental constraints continuously change over time. Water kefir provides a tractable model to investigate how multispecies communities coordinate their metabolic activities during fermentation. Here, we combined time-resolved community profiling, physicochemical measurements, metabolite quantification, and controlled co-culture assays to characterize the dynamics of a water kefir consortium comprising 19 detected microbial species. Our results reveal that water kefir fermentation is not adequately described as a simple succession of independently acting microbial groups. Instead, the community undergoes a reproducible reorganization of its collective metabolism around 20 h of fermentation. This transition marks a shift from an early regime characterized by the accumulation of soluble sugars and ethanol to a later regime dominated by enhanced sugar consumption and lactate production. Controlled interaction assays further showed that bacterial partners can alter carbon-use behaviour in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, highlighting the capacity of interspecies interactions to reshape metabolic phenotypes within the consortium. Together, these results support an ecological view of water kefir fermentation in which community-wide metabolic reorganization emerges from the interplay between microbial interactions, resource availability, and environmental change.

papers.title: Maintenance of restriction-modification system diversity creates pan-immunity
papers.abstract: Bacterial antiviral defense systems are highly diverse and unevenly distributed across populations, such that different strains carry distinct immune repertoires that together form a pan-immune system. Restriction-modification (RM) systems are the most abundant bacterial defense systems and exemplify this architecture, exhibiting remarkable diversity in structure, function, specificity, and efficacy. How and why such diversity is maintained, why weaker systems are not outcompeted, and whether diversity provides benefits beyond protection of individual cells remain unclear. Here, we experimentally tracked bacteria and phages across populations differing in RM diversity. We find no consistent evidence of a trade-off between defense strength and host fitness. Instead, we identify a trade-off between defense strength and horizontal transferability: stronger RM systems are less able to spread between strains, likely because factors that increase defense strength also increase toxicity risk upon transfer to unmethylated hosts. These weaker yet more mobile systems may therefore act as more accessible pan-immune components that bacterial populations can acquire in response to shifting parasite pressures. Furthermore, we show RM systems experience negative frequency-dependent selection, such that common specificities are more readily overcome by phages while rare ones remain protective, causing the benefits of potent systems to erode as they spread. Together, these dynamics maintain RM diversity and explain why weaker systems persist alongside stronger ones. Finally, we show that population-level RM diversity generates collective protection by constraining the emergence of RM-escaping phages and limiting the invasion of bacterial surface mutants that avoid phage adsorption, providing experimental support for the pan-immune model.

papers.title: Genomic and proteomic insights into the virulence of a native Heterorhabditis indica-Photorhabdus akhurstii complex active against Spodoptera spp.
papers.abstract: A native entomopathogenic nematode isolate, Heterorhabditis indica Che4.1, was recovered from soils in Valencia (Spain), and its symbiotic bacterium, Photorhabdus akhurstii Che4.1, was isolated and characterized. Nematode identification was confirmed by ITS and 28S rDNA sequencing, while genome-based analyses supported the taxonomic assignment of the bacterial symbiont. The nematode-bacterium complex exhibited insecticidal activity against Spodoptera exigua and Spodoptera littoralis. H. indica Che4.1 showed an LC of 53.7 infective juveniles (IJs)/mL against S. exigua, comparable to that of the commercial reference Larvanem (54.3 IJs/mL). Against S. littoralis, Che4.1 exhibited an approximately twofold lower LC than Larvanem (77.3 versus 155.9 IJs/mL), with non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals. The complete genome of P. akhurstii Che4.1 consists of a single circular chromosome of 5.66 Mb encoding a diverse repertoire of putative virulence factors, including toxin complex (Tc) components, YenTc-like proteins, Mcf toxins, App-family proteins, Pra/Prb proteins, and chitinases, together with several predicted secondary metabolite biosynthetic gene clusters. LC-MS/MS analyses of bacterial culture supernatants and infected insect cadavers detected multiple predicted virulence-associated proteins, including Tc-related, YenTc-like, App-family, and Pra/Prb proteins. In addition, bacterial cell-free supernatants caused 68.8-81.3% mortality in S. exigua neonates under laboratory conditions. Together, these findings reveal a diverse repertoire of potential virulence determinants in P. akhurstii Che4.1 and demonstrate the insecticidal potential of its native nematodebacterium complex. The performance of H. indica Che4.1 relative to a commercial reference supports further evaluation of this isolate for biological control of Spodoptera spp., particularly under greenhouse and field conditions.

papers.title: A tetracycline-inducible promoter for gene expression in Gram-negative bacteria including Acinetobacter baumannii
papers.abstract: Carbohydrate inducible promoters on expression plasmids are widely used for biotechnology and basic science research. However, using carbohydrates for inducers has drawbacks including influencing bacterial metabolism, the inducer being used as a carbon source by the bacteria, high background expression, and only a subset of cells experiencing promoter activation. Furthermore, some bacteria including the pathogen Acinetobacter baumannii currently lack good carbohydrate-inducible promoters. To address this issue, a tetracycline-inducible promoter, PtetB, isolated from A. baumannii was cloned and evaluated in a number of important bacteria: Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Pseudomonas fluorescens, and Serratia marcescens. A highly sensitive luxCDABE reporter was used to evaluate promoter activity. S. marcescens strains with elevated and reduced cyclic-AMP levels were used to evaluate the impact of cAMP on PtetB function. The PtetB promoter was induced over 800-fold in A. baumannii and 10-750-fold inducible in the other tested species. Background expression was lower from PtetB in the pseudomonads than previously described carbohydrate inducible promoters. Data indicated that the PtetB promoter system may be a useful tool for future basic science research with the tested bacteria.

papers.title: Shedding light on the virome of Caliothrips phaseoli, an emergent pest in peanut
papers.abstract: The bean thrips, Caliothrips phaseoli, is an emergent pest affecting peanut production. Thus, gaining a deeper understanding of the naturally occurring viral populations associated with this insect is of major importance, as such knowledge could support the design of novel pest management strategies that are both ecologically responsible and sustainable over the long term. In this study, we performed the first RNA high-throughput sequencing (HTS) analysis of C. phaseoli to unravel its virome, discovering a wide number of novel RNA viruses. Our HTS analysis revealed the presence of 31 viral segments, corresponding to 18 viruses, including double-stranded RNA viruses as well as positive- and negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses. All these are novel viruses and cover multiple viral lineages belonging to diverse families. Overall, these results indicates that C. phaseoli hides a complex virome. The findings presented here provide an important framework for subsequent studies aimed at understanding the ecological significance, evolutionary patterns, and possible use of these viruses as components of biologically based management programs for this emerging peanut pest.

papers.title: MnSOD Diversifies, while FeSOD Dominates Superoxide Defense in Cyanobacteria
papers.abstract: Cyanobacteria are unique among prokaryotes in possessing photosynthetic thylakoid membranes enclosing an internal lumen, where superoxide production is expected to be substantial. Thylakoid-associated superoxide dismutases (SODs) would seem the obvious first line of defense, yet many cyanobacteria rely instead on a single soluble cytoplasmic enzyme, raising the question of what role thylakoid-associated SOD isoforms actually play. Using Cyanothece sp. PCC 7425, which encodes both a cytoplasmic FeSOD and a thylakoid-associated MnSOD, we combined sequence analysis, structural, genetics, and biochemical approaches to characterise FeSOD and MnSOD cellular localisation and assess each enzyme's contribution to superoxide defense. Cyanobacterial MnSODs display diverse N-terminal architectures, consistent with soluble, transmembrane, or lipid-anchored forms, yet contribute only modestly to superoxide defense in Cyanothece PCC 7425 and, very likely, across cyanobacteria broadly. Soluble FeSOD instead provides the major line of defense, showing that thylakoid association does not guarantee physiological importance. This predominance of a cytoplasmic enzyme highlights the central role of cytoplasmic superoxide detoxification, consistent with superoxide being generated mainly at the PSI acceptor side, and extends to the chloroplast stroma of plants. Our findings support a model in which SOD distribution reflects metal availability, enzyme properties, and subcellular organisation : FeSOD protects the compartment harbouring the main targets of PSI-associated superoxide, whereas MnSOD is retained where thylakoid association offers additional local protection, but becomes dispensable when the local ROS burden is limited. Spatial matching between superoxide production, antioxidant localisation, and target vulnerability may thus shape the diversification and maintenance of antioxidant systems across cyanobacteria and chloroplasts.

papers.title: Chronic stress remodels gut bacterial ecology and polysaccharide metabolism with neuroendocrine consequences despite unchanged behavior
papers.abstract: The gut-microbiome-brain axis (GMBA) links the gut and brain through metabolic, immunological, and neuroendocrine pathways, and can become dysregulated during psychological stress (PS). While previous studies primarily infer microbial function and use physical stressors that incompletely model human PS, here, functional multi-omics was applied to a chronic social-isolation mouse model. Although isolation caused no measurable behavioral changes, brain proteomics revealed stress-associated molecular responses. Taxonomic and short-chain fatty acid analyses suggested limited microbiome changes; however, metaproteomics uncovered sex-specific restructuring of bacterial ecology and carbohydrate-active enzymes. In females, isolation increased Petralouisia muris proteins involved in bacterial microcompartment metabolism and {beta}-glucuronidases across Lachnospiraceae taxa. Enriched {beta}-glucuronidase abundance coincided with reduced circulating glucuronides and altered brain estrogen-receptor activity, suggesting a microbial deconjugation-host estrogen-signaling interaction. These findings demonstrate that functional GMBA alterations may precede or occur independently of overt behavioral phenotypes and highlight the value of direct functional profiling in PS.

papers.title: EF-P-resolved ribosome stalling and collision trigger Rae1-mediated mRNA decay
papers.abstract: Ribosome stalling compromises proteome integrity and cellular fitness, and requires efficient mechanisms to eliminate problematic mRNAs and rescue blocked ribosomes. We previously identified Rae1 as an endoribonuclease that cleaves mRNAs at the tail end of stalled ribosomes to promote mRNA degradation in Bacillus subtilis. Here, we show that Rae1 has a broader role in the quality control of mRNAs that encounter translation problems. Global 5-end sequencing identified 31 previously unknown Rae1 cleavage sites, many of them associated with ribosome pausing at polyproline motifs in the absence of elongation factor P (EF-P). We also demonstrate that Rae1 cleaves mRNAs with ribosomes stalled on truncated transcripts lacking a stop-codon (non-stop mRNAs), provided that the transcript is sufficiently long to accommodate multiple collided ribosomes. Rae1 cleavage depends on a cytosine-poor context at the cut site, showing that both ribosome collisions and RNA sequence at the cleavage site govern the ability of Rae1 to promote the removal of stalled ribosomes from mRNA.

papers.title: Coronavirus nucleocapsid proteins differentially antagonize RIG-I-like receptor signaling to shape pathogenicity
papers.abstract: Coronaviruses cause human infections with divergent clinical outcomes. Viral proteins likely play important roles in the severity of human diseases but are poorly defined. In this study, we discovered that viral nucleocapsid (N) proteins from various human coronaviruses have distinct abilities to antagonize human innate immune responses. N proteins from more pathogenic coronaviruses, such as SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2, have more potent activities specifically against human RIG-I-like receptor (RLR) activation than less pathogenic coronaviruses including OC43 and HKU1. Mechanistically, the SARS-CoV-2 N protein interacts with RLR pathway viral RNA sensors MDA5 and RIG-I and inhibits their interaction with MAVS. The CTD of SARS-CoV-2 N protein is an important region for RLR antagonism. Consequently, N proteins from more pathogenic coronaviruses promote viral replication more effectively than N proteins from less pathogenic coronaviruses. Blocking N protein function may be a promising antiviral strategy.

papers.title: The essential lipoprotein maturation enzyme Lgt is required for flagellar and membrane integrity in Helicobacter pylori
papers.abstract: Pre-prolipoprotein phosphatidylglycerol diacylglyceryl transferase (Lgt) catalyzes the first step in the lipoprotein modification pathway and is essential for growth and viability of Helicobacter pylori. We explored the fate of H. pylori cells under Lgt depletion conditions to obtain insight into Lgt function on morphology and physiology. Downregulation of lgt expression led to growth arrest and a heterogenous population of small rod-shaped cells and small round cells with spiky protrusions, a loose outer membrane and disintegrated flagella. H. pylori overcomes a defect in lipoprotein modification through alteration of its gene expression profile resulting in so-called revertants. Outer membrane protein synthesis, carbon metabolism and nutrient uptake was reduced, and protein translation and flagellar biogenesis increased. Lgt specific regulation was observed in phospholipid biosynthesis resulting in an initial increase in cardiolipin followed by an increase in lysophospholipids at the time of adaptation. Suppressors of {Delta}lgt that were selected on solid media under restrictive conditions either lacked chromosomal mutations or had mutations in the cagUT-tetR regulon controlling the expression of lgt. A suppressor without mutations had an altered expression profile that led to downregulation of a DNA methyltransferase and upregulation of HP_0014, a motility associated glycosyltransferase family protein. Transmission electron microscopy and single cell video microscopy showed that a subpopulation of cells is motile in the revertant while the suppressor regained full motility with higher average speed compared to the wild type strain. Overall, our data show that lipoprotein modification by Lgt is important for membrane and flagellar integrity and that the heterogenous character of H. pylori cultures allows individual cells to overcome this cell envelope stress and survive. Our findings are important for antibacterial development strategies targeting essential integral membrane enzymes involved in lipoprotein modification and stimulate exploration of synergetic activity between known antibiotics and novel antibacterial agents targeting novel cellular pathways.

papers.title: Repurposing clofarabine against enteric pathogens via metabolic starvation
papers.abstract: Enteropathogenic and enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EPEC/EHEC) cause severe global diarrhoeal disease, exacerbated by rising antimicrobial resistance. Pathogenesis relies on "attaching and effacing" lesions, where bacteria generate actin pedestals to adhere, replicate, and destroy intestinal microvilli. To identify novel anti-virulence candidates targeting this process, we conducted a high-throughput phenotypic screen quantifying pedestal formation via high-content fluorescence microscopy. We identified the anticancer nucleotide analogue clofarabine as a potent inhibitor of EPEC growth and pathogenesis. Distinct from its oncology mechanism - inducing DNA chain termination and apoptosis - clofarabine competes with bacterial ATP-dependent processes to impede gene transcription, protein synthesis, and Type III Secretion System (T3SS) function. Remarkably, EPEC counteracts this inhibition by cleaving clofarabine, enabling restored protein synthesis and resumed growth. Furthermore, we report for the first time that clofarabine suppresses protein translation in human monocytes, suggesting an uncharacterised translational impact on mammalian cells. These findings reveal host and bacterial translation as interconnected vulnerabilities to purine antimetabolites, offering a novel strategy to disarm enteric pathogens while uncovering a bacterial enzymatic mechanism for neutralizing host-targeted therapeutics.

papers.title: Comparison of intracellular and encapsidated viral RNA reveals selective constraints on reovirus recombination
papers.abstract: Recombination can generate genetic diversity among RNA viruses; yet, mechanisms governing recombination for segmented, double-stranded RNA viruses remain poorly understood. Reovirus genomes contain ten segments of double-stranded RNA. Previous analyses suggested low rates of reovirus RNA recombination and led to a proposed mechanism of recombination during minus-strand synthesis. These analyses focused on recombination events detected in genomic double-stranded RNA extracted from purified viral particles. In the current study, we looked deeper into the origins of the observed recombination events by assaying total cellular material, which comprises viral genomic material, as well as replication intermediates, mRNAs, and products of recombination that may not be eligible for packaging into virus particles. Intracellular viral RNA, which is almost exclusively plus-strand RNA, exhibited substantially higher recombination frequency than particle-associated double-stranded RNA. The diversity and frequency of identified junctions were more similar among samples of a given type (intracellular or virion-encapsidated) from distinct infections than between distinct sample types from the same infection. Although potential recombination sites are widely distributed across the genome, a more limited set was used in junctions in packaged viral RNA than in intracellular viral RNA. Together, these observations suggest recombination may occur more frequently than previously recognized during reovirus infection, and many such events likely occur during plus-strand synthesis. However, recombination products generated during viral transcription may be selectively incorporated into viral particles.

papers.title: Commensal Bacteria in the Gut Microbiome Encode Previously Unrecognized Aromatic Hydrocarbon Catabolic Machinery
papers.abstract: Introduction. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) toxicology has been primarily defined by host metabolic bioactivation to reactive intermediates. Yet ingested PAHs and biliary-delivered metabolites also enter the intestinal lumen, where they encounter the gut microbiota, an additional but understudied metabolic compartment that may alter toxicant fate. Although PAH interactions are well characterized in environmental microbes, resulting in defined enzymatic pathways for their catabolism, whether gut commensal organisms express related machinery in vivo remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we used an oral murine-exposure model of naphthalene and integrated compartment-resolved 16S rRNA gene profiling, global metaproteomics, and chemoproteomics to resolve the PAH-processing repertoire of the gut microbiota and its spatial distribution. Results. Naphthalene, a common environmental toxicant and representative PAH, elicited a compartment-dependent functional response that was most pronounced in the large intestine. Distally, exposure was associated with 2,386 differential proteins and accounted for 48.4% of metaproteomic variation, compared with 7.9% of 16S rRNA gene compositional variation. The small intestine showed a reduced proteomic response, with 994 differentially abundant proteins. Hydrocarbon catabolic markers showed a 4.8-fold distal expansion (36 to 172 proteins), including the naphthalene-catabolic nahE, proteins associated with phenylacetate, {beta}-ketoadipate, catechol/TOL, and anaerobic CoA-linked redox machinery. The small-intestinal repertoire decreased from 19 to 14 proteins, though aromatic-catabolic markers doubled, indicating a selective expansion. Critically, these homologs concentrated in Lachnospiraceae, a gut family that is prevalent in humans, primarily known for anaerobic fermentation, with no priorly described PAH-processing capacity. An uncultured Acetatifactor showed the largest hydrocarbon hits (14 to 82 protein increase), with additional contributions from Kineothrix, Eisenbergiella, and Petralouisia. Chemoproteomics, using a naphthalene-based probe, revealed enrichment of an orthogonal proteome of proteins interacting with naphthalene, capturing 171 small-intestinal and 67 large-intestinal proteins that were undetected in the global metaproteomes. Conclusions. Gut commensals express homologs of aromatic-hydrocarbon catabolic enzymes characterized in environmental microorganisms, and naphthalene amplifies this repertoire most strongly in the large intestine. The decoupling of taxonomic structure, expressed-protein representation, and probe engagement identifies a functional dimension of PAH exposure that composition-based profiling does not resolve and positions microbiome variation as a candidate modifier of PAH metabolic fate.

papers.title: Establishing genetic tractability in Jeongeupia sacculi HS-3: disruption of rpoS hinders biofilm formation
papers.abstract: Jeongeupia sacculi (HS-3) is a novel {beta}-proteobacterium with a unique multicellular life cycle. The genetic tractability and mechanisms underlying differentiation are unknown. Here, we adapt a method of homologous recombination for genetic modification in HS-3 and generate a disruption mutant of rpoS, which encodes the alternative sigma factor{sigma} S commonly associated with general stress response or major behavioral switches. We then characterize phenotypes associated with rpoS disruption. Under low-nutrient conditions, rpoS disruption reduced Congo red binding, consistent with rpoS acting as a regulator of low-nutrient response by upregulating production of biofilm-associated materials. Surprisingly, rpoS disruption did not significantly alter survival in response to other stressors in general stress response assays tested. Our work establishes a method for genetic manipulation in HS-3 and enables future investigation into the life cycle of HS-3, including whether rpoS has a role in differentiation triggered by low-nutrient response.

papers.title: Macrophage DYRK1A is broadly required for bacterial phagocytosis
papers.abstract: Listeria monocytogenes is an intracellular foodborne pathogen that causes the serious illness listeriosis. Macrophages are central to the outcome of L. monocytogenes infection, yet the host requirements that facilitate bacterial uptake remain incompletely understood. In a previous genome-wide screen for macrophage factors that influence L. monocytogenes infection, we identified the macrophage kinase DYRK1A, which has been studied largely in neurodevelopment and cancer models but has no described role in bacterial infection. Here we show that DYRK1A promotes efficient internalization of L. monocytogenes by macrophages. Using several complementary approaches, we find that DYRK1A acts early during infection, primarily by promoting bacterial attachment to the macrophage surface. Transcriptomics of DYRK1A-deficient macrophages revealed reduced abundance of transcripts encoding membrane-associated proteins and components of innate immune and phagocytic pathways, suggesting a transcriptional basis for the attachment defect. Consistent with the broad nature of these changes, the role of DYRK1A extended beyond uptake of L. monocytogenes to the Fc receptor pathway and to additional bacterial species spanning multiple genera, establishing a broad role in macrophage phagocytosis. Together, these findings define a previously undescribed role for the host factor DYRK1A in macrophage phagocytosis and expand the function of DYRK1A beyond its established roles to innate immune defense.

papers.title: A chimeric infection program and epigenetic conflict underpin endogenous giant virus latency
papers.abstract: Giant endogenous viral elements (GEVEs) are ubiquitous in eukaryotic genomes, but how the virus adapts to the host and is capable of reactivation despite host defense mechanisms remains unclear. Here we examined this process in the green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and its latent giant virus, punuivirus, which is integrated into the host genome. We reveal a chimeric genomic architecture in which punuivirus latency genes are enriched in spliceosomal introns and 6-methyladenine marks, mirroring host transcriptional regulation, while virulence genes are predominantly controlled by a conserved viral promoter. Using single-cell RNA-seq, we show that nearly 70% of cells express viral transcripts, but only a small subpopulation commits to viral production, expressing virulence genes with host transcriptional shutoff. Moreover, we find that the intact punuivirus GEVE remains refractory to host 5-methylcytosine (5mC) silencing, whereas a naturally occurring deletion variant is associated with widespread 5mC accumulation across the GEVE and elsewhere in the host genome. The deleted region encodes a highly expressed ten-eleven translocation dioxygenase (TET), and epigenetic profiling of intact and deletion strains implicates this GEVE gene in removing 5mC marks, thereby maintaining the virus in a transcriptionally permissive latent state. Our study provides novel insights into the molecular underpinnings of host-virus co-existence in a giant virus-alga interaction.

papers.title: Multilayer analysis reveals extensive hidden population complexity in a dairy starter microbiome comprising few species
papers.abstract: The genomic and epigenomic complexity of microbiomes with low species richness remains poorly characterized. Here, we integrated 111 non-redundant isolate genomes with deep long-read metagenomics to investigate an undefined mesophilic dairy starter. Closely related isolates harboured distinct combinations of features associated with fermentation traits and phage defence, including surface polysaccharide genotypes, plasmids, prophages, defence systems, and methylation profiles. Metagenomics revealed additional elements and inferred host associations. However, the limited overlap between approaches across core-genome lineages and accessory repertoires underscored complementary but incomplete recovery, to the extent that the dominant metagenomic cell wall polysaccharide genotype (29.6% abundance) was absent from isolates. Metagenomic methylation signatures supported 36 species-level plasmid-host assignments, corroborated by isolate genomes in nine of ten testable cases. Our findings revealed extensive combinatorial diversity hidden from either approach alone, providing a plausible molecular basis for phage resilience, while likely representing only a lower bound on population complexity.

papers.title: Immunomodulatory RIG-I Agonist SLR14 Confers Protection Against a Range of Highly Pathogenic Negative Sense RNA viruses
papers.abstract: Emerging and re-emerging zoonotic RNA viruses, including filoviruses, henipaviruses and Rift Valley Fever virus (RVFV), pose a significant threat to human health. Due to their epidemic potential and high pathogenicity, these viruses are categorized as WHO priority pathogens, yet we still lack effective medical countermeasures (MCMs) against most of these dangerous pathogens, supporting that host-directed antivirals will be advantageous for broadly acting MCMs. Here we assessed the antiviral efficacy of SLR14, an immunomodulatory stem-loop RNA that activates RIG-I, for its activity against a panel of highly pathogenic viruses. SLR14 treatment provided broad-spectrum protection, markedly reducing infection with Ebola virus (EBOV), Marburg virus, and Sudan virus in human primary monocyte-derived macrophages, and Nipah virus replication in iPSC-derived endothelial cells, whether administered prophylactically or therapeutically. In vivo, a single dose of SLR14 protected mice against lethal RVFV infection when administered prophylactically, and, notably, retained significant efficacy when administered up to two days post-infection. Therapeutic SLR14 administration also improved survival rates of EBOV-infected mice. Although EBOV infection and SLR14 treatment activated overlapping innate immune pathways in human macrophages, viral infection induced a nonprotective response, whereas SLR14 elicited a well-regulated, markedly stronger and protective interferon-stimulated and inflammatory gene signature while avoiding prolonged IFN gene upregulation. Our data identify SLR14 as a potent host-directed therapeutic with broad antiviral efficacy against some of the most lethal viral pathogens.

papers.title: Predicted structure of the 89-kDa invasion-tip protein of Holospora obtusa, an endonuclear symbiont of Paramecium caudatum, suggests a pH-dependent conformational change
papers.abstract: The endonuclear symbiont Holospora obtusa invades the macronucleus of Paramecium caudatum using an infectious-form invasion-tip containing a major 89-kDa periplasmic protein implicated in escape from the host digestive vacuole and macronuclear invasion. Sequence-based analyses placed this protein within a Holospora-specific family and predicted an N-terminal membrane-anchoring module and a long alpha-helical C-terminal region. AlphaFold2 modeling followed by molecular dynamics indicated that the C-terminal region forms an antiparallel, spectrin-repeat-like helical solenoid containing a localized three-helix coiled-coil. The protein exhibits a large pH-dependent charge difference, becoming 55 units more positive at pH 4 than at pH 7. Independent simulations at these pH values differed mainly in the relative orientation of the N-terminal core and C-terminal rod, described by DynDom as an approximately 35 degrees rigid-body rotation about a hinge centered on Gly291. However, none of the nearby glutamates (Glu273, Glu275, and Glu302) formed a pH-dependent salt bridge, and no specific protonation-dependent interaction responsible for the conformational difference was identified. We nonetheless propose, as a testable hypothesis, that acidification of the digestive vacuole may promote this reorientation, thereby repositioning the N-terminal membrane-anchoring module at the bacterial surface as an early step toward escape from the vacuole.
